title: Year 4: year close
hook: the summit sit, looking back over a year that kept asking questions, from a king in a forest to a hymn that wonders who really knows

segments.voice: Yesterday, the last summit sit: the regional traditions, and what each place carries, from palm leaves to walnuts. Today, the whole year at once.

Who really knows? The hymn of creation in the Rig Veda asks it near its end, and then, in paraphrase, says this about the one who watches over everything from the highest heaven: perhaps he knows, or perhaps he does not know. That hymn stands in the scripture, question and all. And from the top of year four, it doesn't sit alone. This whole year kept stopping at questions. Today, the year close, told by the questions it asked.
screen: `WHO REALLY KNOWS?` → `PERHAPS HE DOES NOT KNOW.` → `A YEAR OF QUESTIONS.`

segments.voice: It opened with one. A king who'd lost his kingdom and a merchant thrown out by his family asked a sage: we know these things have left us, so why doesn't knowing help? The whole Devi Mahatmya is the answer. Then the questions got sharper. The schools of thought asked how anyone knows anything at all, and the path let each school answer in its own way, ranking none. The Nyaya Sutra, near its opening, names the means of knowing. The Vedas asked in their own voice: what covered it, where, in whose keeping? Then came the women, and several of them were remembered for a question. Gargi asked Yajnavalkya what the world is woven on, and when he told her to stop, she came back with two more. Maitreyi asked what she'd do with wealth that can't make her immortal. Damayanti found her husband by sending out a question only he would understand. Even the regions brought one: a Kashmiri teacher, Abhinavagupta, asking why a sad play leaves its audience lighter. A tradition could have smoothed these over and kept only the answers. This one kept the questions inside its sacred texts: in the king's mouth, in Gargi's, in a Vedic hymn. And some are never closed. The hymn of creation doesn't resolve its last line. It ends on perhaps. So that's year four from the top: the goddess, Shiva, the schools, the three paths, the Vedas, Ayurveda as a lens, the women, the regions. And running through them, people asking honest questions out loud, and the tradition keeping them.
screen: `IT OPENED WITH ONE QUESTION.` · `THE SCHOOLS ASKED HOW WE KNOW.` · `GARGI, MAITREYI, DAMAYANTI ASKED.` · `THE QUESTIONS WERE KEPT.` · then, large: `IT ENDS ON PERHAPS.`

segments.voice: Let one real question rise, something you don't know the answer to, about your life, or about God, or about anything, and let it sit beside you the way the hymn lets its last line sit. Each time the mind starts building an answer, come back to the breath, and to the question, still open. If you pray, you can hold it before God, or the goddess, as it is.
Year four. The goddess, Shiva, the schools of thought, the Vedas, the women and the regions, looked at from the top by the questions they asked. Today's word.
Your line: Year 4, year close. Tomorrow, the last day of the year, and the ranges ahead. Day one thousand four hundred twenty-five.

howItsDone: Hindu traditions keep questions inside their texts: the Upanishads hold dialogues between teachers and questioners, and the hymn of creation, with its open last line, is chanted as part of the Rig Veda.

chat.says: Doesn't a sacred text have to give answers, not questions?
options: Not this one: the Rig Veda's creation hymn ends on perhaps, and was kept that way.
Yes, which is why the creation hymn's open last line was cut from the Rig Veda.
Yes, every question in the old texts is answered by the very next verse.
chat.meaning: The tradition kept questions inside its texts; the hymn of creation ends on perhaps he knows, or perhaps he does not know.

Rig Veda.meaning: the earliest of the Vedas, a collection of hymns

Devi Mahatmya.meaning: a text in praise of the Goddess

Nyaya Sutra.meaning: the founding text of Nyaya, a school of logic

Yajnavalkya.meaning: the Upanishadic sage questioned by Gargi and Maitreyi

Abhinavagupta.meaning: a Kashmiri teacher who wrote on art and feeling
